summary: H.R. 1526, known as the No Rogue Rulings Act of 2025 (NORRA of 2025), limits the power of U.S. district courts to issue injunctions. Under the bill, a district court generally cannot issue an injunction unless it applies only to the specific parties involved in the particular case. However, an exception is made for cases brought by two or more states in different circuits challenging an executive branch action; these cases must be referred to a randomly selected three-judge panel, which may issue broader injunctions based on specific criteria.

affected_groups.effect: Their authority to issue nationwide or broadly applicable injunctions is restricted.
If two or more states in different circuits challenge an executive action, their case goes to a special three-judge panel instead of a single judge.
Any injunctive relief they receive from a district court will be limited to the specific parties in the case.

key_provisions: Prohibits U.S. district courts from issuing injunctions unless they apply only to the parties of the particular case before the court and non-parties represented by that party.
Requires cases brought by two or more states located in different circuits that challenge an executive branch action to be referred to a randomly selected three-judge panel.

Allows the three-judge panel to issue an injunction that would otherwise be prohibited, considering factors such as the interest of justice, risk of irreparable harm to non-parties, and the separation of powers.

Provides that appeals of orders granting or denying injunctive relief from the three-judge panel may go to the circuit embracing the district or directly to the Supreme Court, at the preference of the party.
missing_information: The source material does not provide historical context, potential budgetary impacts, or data on how often district courts currently issue broader injunctions.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 1526, known as the No Rogue Rulings Act of 2025 (NORRA of 2025), limits the power of U.S. district courts to issue injunctions. Under the bill, a district court generally cannot issue an injunction unless it applies only to the specific parties involved in the particular case. However, an exception is made for cases brought by two or more states in different circuits challenging an executive branch action; these cases must be referred to a randomly selected three-judge panel, which may issue broader injunctions based on specific criteria.
summary_detail.significance: The bill changes how federal courts can issue injunctions by restricting single district courts from issuing orders that affect people outside the specific parties of a lawsuit, while setting up a special three-judge panel process for multi-state challenges against executive branch actions.
